evidence:
[S1] MTM_Organizational_Change_Detailed_Revised.pdf — page 4
Forces that create the need for change External forces General environment: social, cultural, demographic, political, economic and technological shifts. Business environment: industry changes, competitors and changing customer demands. Core idea: the organization must adjust when the outside world makes the current system less effective. Internal forces Low performance or declining results. Low employee satisfaction or recurring conflict. A new mission, strategy or leadership direction. question: What economic concerns can make employees resist organizational change?
evidence:
[S1] MTM_Organizational_Change_Detailed_Revised.pdf — page 8
Individual resistance: economic reasons Job security: employees may fear automation, restructuring or role reduction. Skill obsolescence: a new technology can reduce the value of expertise built over many years. Economic loss: employees may anticipate lower income, overtime, benefits or future earning power. Reduced incentives: a new system may remove familiar rewards or make targets feel harder to achieve. Managerial response: clarify the real impact, retrain where possible, and avoid pretending there are no trade-offs.
reference: Economic resistance can stem from fear of job loss, skills becoming obsolete, reduced income or benefits, and the loss of familiar incentives. [S1]

question: Name the six approaches for overcoming resistance to change.
evidence:
[S1] MTM_Organizational_Change_Detailed_Revised.pdf — page 12
Overcoming resistance to change: six approaches Education Explain why and how. Facts, rationale, training and communication reduce misunderstanding. Participation Involve those affected. People contribute to the design, increasing information quality and ownership. Facilitation Help people adapt. Training, coaching, time, resources and emotional support reduce transition cost. Negotiation Exchange for cooperation. Offer incentives or concessions when a group has real power and expects to lose. Manipulation Selective influence. Withhold or frame information to obtain acceptance. Fast but ethically risky and damaging if exposed. Coercion Use authority or threat. Can force rapid compliance in urgent situations, but may create fear, resentment and low commitment.
reference: The six approaches are education, participation, facilitation, negotiation, manipulation, and coercion. The document cautions that manipulation and coercion can create ethical or trust-related problems. [S1]

question: Define a digital image in terms of f(x,y).
evidence:
[S1] Unit-1 Image Fundamentals.pdf — page 1
What is an image? An image is a two-dimensional function that represents a measure of some characteristic such as brightness or colour of a viewed scene. An image is a projection of a 3D scene into a 2D projection plane. It can be defined as a two-variable function f (x, y) where for each position (x, y) in the projection plane, f (x, y) defines the light intensity at this point. An image is defined as a two-dimensional function, f(x, y), x, y are spatial coordinates, and the amplitude of f at any pair of coordinates (x, y) is called the intensity or gray level of the image at that point. When x, y and the amplitude values of f are all finite, discrete quantities, we call the image a digital image.
reference: An image is a two-dimensional function f(x,y), where x and y are spatial coordinates and f gives the intensity at a point. It is a digital image when the coordinates and intensity values are finite, discrete quantities. [S1]

question: What is the difference between image sampling and quantization?
evidence:
[S1] Unit-1 Image Fundamentals.pdf — page 6
Basic Concept in Image Sampling and Quantization There are numerous ways to acquire images, but our objective in all is the same: to generate digital images from sensed data. The output of most sensors is a continuous voltage waveform whose amplitude and spatial behavior are related to the physical phenomenon being sensed. To create a digital image, we need to convert the continuous sensed data into a digital format. This requires two processes: sampling and quantization. Basic Concepts in Sampling and Quantization Figure 2.16(a) shows a continuous image f that we want to convert to digital form. An image may be continuous with respect to the x- and y-coordinates, and also in amplitude. To convert the continuous function f(x,y) to digital form, we need to sample the function in both co-ordinates and in amplitude. Digitizing the co-ordinates value is called sampling. Digitizing the amplitude value is called quantization.
reference: Sampling digitizes the spatial coordinate values of an image, while quantization digitizes its amplitude or intensity values. Both are needed to turn continuous sensed data into a digital image. [S1]

question: How do gamma values below, equal to and above one affect a power-law transformation?

question: Which interface features help place the user in control?
evidence:
[S1] Unit-6-UID_JIeh32ZBED(1).pdf — page 5
Place the User in Control • Define interaction modes in a way that does not force a user into unnecessary or undesired actions. For example, if spell check is selected in a word-processor menu, the software moves to a spell-checking mode. • Provide for flexible interaction. For example, software might allow a user to interact via keyboard commands, mouse movement, a digitizer pen, a multitouch screen, or voice recognition commands. • Allow user interaction to be interruptible and undoable. Eg. The user should also be able to “undo” any action. • Design for direct interaction with objects that appear on the screen.
reference: The notes recommend avoiding unnecessary interaction modes, supporting flexible interaction methods, making user actions interruptible and undoable, and enabling direct interaction with on-screen objects. [S1]

question: Name and describe the four user interface design models.
evidence:
[S1] Unit-6-UID_JIeh32ZBED(1).pdf — page 9
User Interface Design Models ◼User model — a profile of all end users of the system ◼Design model — a design realization of the user model ◼Mental model (system perception) — the user’s mental image of what the interface is ◼Implementation model — the interface “look and feel” coupled with supporting information that describe interface syntax and semantics
reference: The user model profiles the system’s end users; the design model realizes that user model; the mental model represents the user’s perception of the interface; and the implementation model describes its look, feel, syntax and semantics. [S1]
